title: The Hospital
strapline: Ambulance at the doors, a ward of poorly patients, and a whole team of doctors, nurses and porters making people better.
intent: Hospitals can be frightening or mysterious to young children, and playing out a whole hospital — wards, ambulance, X-rays, operations — helps them process and feel calm about a big, important place.
The hospital is packed with real community helpers — doctors, nurses, paramedics, porters — building knowledge of the many people who care for us when we are unwell.
Caring for poorly patients, comforting them and explaining what will happen grows deep empathy, nurture and communication.
Running a ward is full of mathematics — temperatures and numbers on charts, counting patients and medicines, measuring, timing, sorting who needs what.
Children learn genuine, reassuring knowledge about being unwell, being cared for, and getting better, and gain the language to talk about their bodies.
Rich vocabulary and knowledge grow — hospital, ambulance, patient, bandage, X-ray, temperature, recover, care.
implementation: Set up a hospital with more than one room — a waiting area, a ward with beds, an ambulance outside, an X-ray light box, medical kits and charts.
Take a patient role so children diagnose, treat, comfort and explain: 'I've hurt my arm and I'm a bit scared — what's going to happen to me?'
Model the caring, informative talk: 'Let's check your temperature and write it on your chart. The doctor's going to make you feel better.'
Bring in maths through the play — read and record numbers on charts, count patients and pills, measure bandages, time the treatments.
Weave in real, reassuring knowledge — what an ambulance does, why we have X-rays, how the body heals — and read hospital-themed stories.
Add appointment books, prescriptions and patient notes for real writing, and let the drama grow — a new baby on the ward, an emergency arriving, a patient going home well.
key_questions: I've hurt my arm and I'm a bit scared — what's going to happen to me?
Let's check your temperature — what number shall we write on the chart?
How many patients are on the ward today?
How long shall we time this treatment for?
What does the ambulance do, and who drives it?

Children meet the many community helpers who care for us when we are unwell.
Children comfort patients and explain what will happen, growing deep empathy and nurture.
Children read and record numbers on charts, count patients and pills, measure and time.
Children gain reassuring knowledge about being cared for and getting better, and words for their bodies.

Appointment books, prescriptions and patient notes for real writing.
Charts to read and record temperatures and numbers.
A growing storyline — a new baby, an emergency arriving, a patient going home well.
Hospital-themed stories to read alongside the play.

playing_exploring: Children play out a big, sometimes worrying real place, taking charge of it through nurturing role play.
They explore the equipment and the many roles of the hospital team.
active_learning: Children take the care of their patients seriously, seeing each treatment and recovery through.
creating_thinking: Children diagnose and solve each patient's problem, and take on reassuring knowledge about illness, care and getting better.
